vignette:
He is 68 years old, European, married, and has spent much of his adult life in politics, a profession that has trained him to speak calmly under pressure and to keep moving even when he is angry, tired, or afraid. Before the accident, he describes himself as someone who trusted his body to carry him through long days of meetings, public appearances, and travel. He was used to being on stage, answering difficult questions, and projecting steadiness. That sense of control changes in a single moment when he is involved in a life-threatening accident that leaves him convinced he is going to die.

He still returns to that moment with a kind of stunned disbelief. He remembers the sudden violence of it, the noise, the shock in his body, and then the awful realization that there is no easy way out. In the weeks afterward, he finds that the memory does not stay in the past where it belongs. It intrudes while he is sitting in his office, while he is reading briefing papers, while he is having dinner with his wife. He can be in the middle of a conversation and suddenly feel his chest tighten and his mind go blank, as if part of him has been pulled back into the scene. At night he wakes abruptly, disoriented, with his heart racing, and for a few seconds he does not know where he is.

As a politician, he is expected to remain composed in public, and he works hard to preserve that image. He returns to duties sooner than he probably should, telling himself that he cannot afford to look fragile. On the outside he appears capable and controlled, but privately he is increasingly organized around fear. He avoids the road where the accident occurred and chooses longer routes without admitting why. He does not like being a passenger now, and he tenses when a driver brakes too suddenly. He finds himself scanning intersections, calculating escape routes, noticing every siren, every loud mechanical sound. The world feels less predictable than it once did, and that change unsettles him deeply.

He becomes more irritable at home, especially with small disruptions that would once have barely registered. His wife notices that he startles easily and that he is not really listening when she speaks because part of his attention is always elsewhere, checking for danger. He is ashamed of the way he snaps and then withdraws, but he also feels unable to stop. After long days, he sits alone instead of joining others, saying he is tired, though what he really feels is drained by the effort of keeping himself together. He has trouble sleeping, and when he does manage to fall asleep, he often wakes unrested, as if his body never fully lets go.

He also notices changes in the way he relates to his work. Where he once enjoyed the pace of campaigning, the crowds, the noise of public life, he now experiences it as overwhelming. Bright lights, sudden questions, and unpredictable schedules leave him tense and exhausted. He still performs, but it costs him more. He becomes preoccupied with the possibility of another accident, another sudden loss of control. This fear narrows his world in quiet ways. He stops taking certain drives. He declines invitations. He lingers at thresholds before entering places that feel too open, too exposed.

At times he is frustrated by himself because he knows he is not behaving like the man he has spent years presenting to the public. He feels embarrassed by his jumpiness, by the way his mind rehearses danger, by his inability to simply move on. Yet he also feels a deep sadness that his life has become organized around surviving rather than living. He speaks of the accident as a dividing line, a point after which he no longer feels quite at ease in his own skin. Even in moments of relative calm, there is a sense that he is bracing for something, holding himself in readiness for the next impact that may never come.
